concerns.concern_text: All three acceptance criteria are entirely unmeasurable. 'Customers love the new checkout' has no numeric threshold or survey methodology. 'Conversion improves significantly' lacks a baseline, target percentage, and measurement window. 'Page feels fast' has no defined performance budget (e.g., LCP, TTI in milliseconds). None of these can be used to objectively pass or fail the release.

There are no measurable success metrics defined anywhere in the project artifacts. A checkout improvement initiative must include at minimum: a conversion rate baseline and target, a specific performance metric with threshold, and a customer satisfaction score (e.g., CSAT, NPS delta). Without these, there is no way to declare success or failure post-launch.

'Checkout Improvements Q1' is a broad umbrella label. The PRD (prd_v2) is the only artifact present and there is no evidence the scope has been decomposed into discrete, independently shippable features. Bundling multiple checkout improvement areas (performance, UX, funnel changes) into one gate increases risk and makes rollback and attribution of outcomes difficult.

No rollback plan is documented in the listed artifacts. Checkout is a revenue-critical flow. Any regression in conversion or stability requires an immediate, documented rollback procedure including feature flags, database migration reversal steps, and an owner responsible for executing it.

agent_responses.reasoning: This project cannot pass the design gate in its current state. The most critical issue is that all acceptance criteria are qualitative and unmeasurable — 'love,' 'significantly,' and 'feels fast' cannot be evaluated against any objective threshold. This means there is literally no way to determine when the project is done or successful. These must be replaced with numeric, time-bound, testable criteria (e.g., 'checkout conversion rate increases from X% to Y% within 30 days of launch, measured against a holdout group'). Additionally, there are no defined success metrics tied to business outcomes. Beyond criteria quality, the scope appears broad without decomposition, and no rollback plan is documented for a revenue-critical flow. I recommend blocking until: (1) all acceptance criteria are rewritten with baselines, targets, and measurement methods; (2) a rollback plan is documented; and (3) scope is explicitly bounded to named feature changes.

concerns.concern_text: All three acceptance criteria are unmeasurable: 'Customers love the new checkout', 'Conversion improves significantly', and 'Page feels fast' have no numeric thresholds, baselines, or testable definitions. There is no way to determine pass/fail at any gate.

No measurable success metric is defined anywhere in the project artifacts. Without a numeric conversion target (e.g., +X% CVR), a Core Web Vitals threshold (e.g., LCP < 2.5s), or a satisfaction score, the project has no objective definition of success.

Checkout improvements touch payment flows. There is no mention of a PCI DSS scope assessment, SAQ categorization, or cardholder data environment impact review in the design artifacts. Any change to checkout pages may affect PCI scope.

No rollback procedure is documented. Checkout is a revenue-critical path; a failed deployment without a rollback plan (e.g., feature flags, blue/green, DB migration rollback) poses significant business risk.

The design artifacts do not describe resilience patterns for downstream dependencies in the checkout critical path (payment processor, inventory, promotions service). No circuit breakers or fallback behaviors are documented.

No timeout configurations are specified for synchronous calls within the checkout flow. Without explicit timeout budgets, a slow dependency can degrade the entire checkout experience and violate any latency goals.

No idempotency strategy is described for order submission or payment mutation endpoints. Duplicate submissions (e.g., from retries or double-clicks) on a checkout flow can result in duplicate charges or orders.

agent_responses.reasoning: This project is blocked at the design gate for two fundamental reasons: (1) all acceptance criteria are qualitative and unmeasurable, making it impossible to define a testable exit condition, and (2) no success metrics with numeric thresholds exist anywhere in the artifacts. Beyond those blocking issues, the design omits critical engineering concerns for a revenue-sensitive checkout flow: no PCI scope review is documented despite touching payment surfaces, no rollback plan exists for a high-stakes release, and standard reliability patterns (circuit breakers, timeouts, idempotency) are absent from the design. The team must revise the PRD to include numeric acceptance criteria (e.g., CVR delta, LCP target, NPS/CSAT threshold), document a PCI impact assessment, define a rollback strategy, and specify timeout/circuit-breaker/idempotency requirements before returning for re-review.

concerns.concern_text: The project involves checkout improvements which almost certainly touches payment card data flows. There is no PCI-DSS scope assessment documented. Any changes to checkout pages, forms, or payment integrations must be reviewed for PCI scope (SAQ-A, SAQ-A-EP, or full PCI-DSS depending on card data handling). Proceeding without this assessment is a blocking compliance risk.

The design artifacts contain no mention of audit logging for security-sensitive checkout actions (e.g., payment initiation, address changes, coupon/discount application, order placement). These actions require tamper-evident audit trails for fraud detection and regulatory compliance.

There is no documented strategy for preventing PII (e.g., customer name, email, shipping address, partial card numbers) from being written to application or performance logs during checkout flow changes. 'Page feels fast' implies performance instrumentation, which is a common vector for PII leakage into logs.

No mention of encryption-at-rest requirements for any new data stores, session state, or order data introduced by this initiative. If any new persistence layer is added as part of checkout improvements, encryption-at-rest must be explicitly scoped.

The design does not address data residency for EU customer checkout data. If the checkout pipeline processes or stores EU customer PII (addresses, emails), the design must confirm that data remains within EU boundaries or that appropriate transfer mechanisms are in place.

No documented legal mechanism (SCCs, adequacy decision, BCRs) for any cross-border transfer of checkout PII. If third-party analytics, A/B testing, or payment processors outside the EU are used, a transfer mechanism must be documented.

agent_responses.reasoning: This checkout improvement project presents multiple blocking and high-severity security and privacy risks. Most critically, checkout changes by definition touch payment flows and must undergo a PCI-DSS scope review before design is approved — none is present in the artifacts. Additionally, there is a complete absence of documentation addressing: audit logging of sensitive financial actions, PII redaction strategies for logs (especially concerning given the performance instrumentation implied by 'page feels fast'), encryption-at-rest for any new data introduced, and GDPR data residency and transfer mechanism requirements for EU customer data. The acceptance criteria are vague ('Customers love the new checkout', 'Conversion improves significantly', 'Page feels fast') and do not include any security or privacy acceptance criteria whatsoever, suggesting security was not incorporated into the design phase. This project must be blocked until a PCI scope assessment is completed and security/privacy design controls are explicitly documented.

concerns.concern_text: All three acceptance criteria are entirely unmeasurable and untestable: 'Customers love the new checkout', 'Conversion improves significantly', and 'Page feels fast' contain no numeric thresholds, baselines, or defined measurement methods. These cannot be used to gate a release or validate success.

There are no quantitative success metrics defined anywhere in the project artifacts. No conversion rate baseline or target delta, no p75/p99 page load time targets, and no CSAT or NPS score defined. FinOps cannot evaluate ROI or cost-per-conversion trade-offs without measurable targets.

Checkout improvements by definition touch payment card data flows. There is no mention of a PCI DSS scope review or assessment in the artifacts. Any change to the checkout page or its integrations must be evaluated for PCI scope impact before proceeding to design.

No cost estimate is present in the project artifacts. Infrastructure, third-party service, or vendor costs associated with the checkout improvements are entirely undocumented. A design gate requires at least a rough order-of-magnitude cost estimate.
No compute or autoscaling cost ceiling is defined. Checkout is a high-traffic critical path; without a cost cap, an infrastructure incident or traffic spike could result in unbounded cloud spend.

The PRD does not identify or document SLA terms for any third-party vendors involved in the checkout flow (e.g., payment processors, fraud detection, address verification services). Vendor SLAs must be on file before design is approved.

agent_responses.reasoning: The project is blocked at the design gate on multiple FinOps and legal dimensions. Most critically, all three acceptance criteria are entirely qualitative and untestable, which is a blocking issue — there is no way to rationally approve spend or release readiness without measurable thresholds. Checkout inherently touches cardholder data, yet there is zero mention of a PCI scope review or DSS assessment, which is a compliance blocker. No cost estimate or cost ceiling exists in any artifact, meaning the project has no financial guardrails. Additionally, no vendor SLAs are documented for the third-party services that are almost certainly part of the checkout stack. The team must return with: (1) numeric acceptance criteria with baselines and targets, (2) a PCI scope impact assessment, (3) a rough cost estimate with autoscaling caps, and (4) documented vendor SLA references before this gate can be re-evaluated.
